matching.reasoningTemplate: Reduced consciousness with depressed respiration and pinpoint pupils is opioid toxicity until proven otherwise.

clinicalPearls: The classic overdose picture is shallow/slow respirations, miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; toxicology can confirm but immediate management is clinical (p.3690).

Pinpoint pupils are characteristic, BUT mydriasis (dilated pupils) appears once significant cerebral anoxia supervenes - dilated pupils do not exclude opioid toxicity in a deteriorating patient (p.3690).

Hypoxia, not the drug itself, is what kills: in opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign changes are secondary to CNS depression or consequent hypoxemia and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression) (p.3748).
Aspiration pneumonia is common in overdose because of loss of the gag reflex (p.3733).
Opioids generally do NOT cause seizures, except in polydrug use, with meperidine, with high-dose tramadol, or in the newborn (p.3690).

Fentanyl and its derivatives may require severalfold higher reversal doses than other opioids, and adulteration of illicit fentanyl with xylazine markedly worsens respiratory suppression (p.3689, p.3733).

Prompt reversal of altered mental status and vital signs within minutes of IV naloxone is virtually diagnostic of opioid poisoning (alongside dextrose for hypoglycemia and flumazenil for benzodiazepine intoxication) (p.3748).
Fluoroquinolones commonly cause false-positive opiate urine screens; rapid urine drug screens are screening-only, prone to false results, and miss agents such as kratom (p.3748).
When naloxone has only a limited effect, suspect a co-ingested sedative - most commonly a benzodiazepine, which has caused fatal overdoses in combination with buprenorphine (p.3691).
harrison.pathophysiology: Opioids act mainly through the mu receptor (also kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin), all G protein-coupled, inhibiting the cAMP system and opening GIRK potassium channels to hyperpolarize and silence neurons. Life-threatening respiratory depression results from opioid-induced insensitivity of brainstem (medullary) respiratory neurons to rising carbon dioxide; analgesia and respiratory depression are mediated by receptors in the periaqueductal grey and medulla oblongata. Untreated, progression goes to respiratory and then cardiovascular collapse and death (p.3733, p.3690).
additionalDifferentials: Cholinergic (muscarinic/nicotinic) poisoning - also causes miosis plus a depressed physiologic state (p.3748)
Sedative-hypnotic / GABAergic poisoning (alcohols, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, GHB) - depressed state, distinguished as naloxone-unresponsive (p.3748)
Sympatholytic poisoning (alpha-2 agonists e.g. clonidine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cardiac glycosides) (p.3747)
Other causes of coma including hypoglycemia (reversed by dextrose) (p.3748)
nonInfectiousMimics: Hypoglycemia (responds to dextrose, mimics opioid coma) (p.3748)
additionalInvestigations: Blood/urine toxicology can confirm a suspected diagnosis but must not delay clinical management (p.3690)
ECG to detect QT prolongation (e.g. methadone), which can cause sudden death (p.3733)
Chest imaging for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, a recognized complication of opioid poisoning (p.3749)
In IV users, screen for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, HIV) and bacterial complications (meningitis, osteomyelitis, abscesses, endocarditis) (p.3733)
redFlags: Dilated pupils in a suspected opioid overdose suggest cerebral anoxia has already occurred (p.3690)
Re-sedation: naloxone lasts only a few hours while most opioids (especially methadone, sustained-release/'toxic time-bomb' formulations) last far longer (p.3691, p.3747)
Methadone-associated QT prolongation and sudden death (p.3733)
Necrosis and limb-loss risk with fentanyl-xylazine injection (p.3733)
harrison.prognosis: Potentially lethal but rapidly reversible if respiratory depression is recognized and supported; untreated overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Opioid use disorder is chronic and relapsing, and most patients relapse during or after detoxification (p.3690, p.3691). Some opioid intoxications can leave delayed diffuse white-matter injury producing a persistent coma syndrome (p.232).
pitfalls: Do not assume normal-sized or dilated pupils exclude opioids - mydriasis does NOT occur until significant brain anoxia supervenes (p.3690).
Significant vital-sign abnormalities do NOT occur in opioid poisoning until there is a marked decrease in level of consciousness, so early near-normal vitals are falsely reassuring (p.3748).

A negative urine drug screen does NOT rule out opioid toxicity (concentration too low, or agent such as kratom not detected); opiate screens also give false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones) (p.3748).

Primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible because it is a partial agonist with increasing antagonist activity at higher doses; failure to respond to naloxone should prompt search for a co-ingested sedative (p.3690-3691).
Be sure a patient is not also withdrawing from alcohol or sedatives, which may be more dangerous to manage than opioid withdrawal (p.3733).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames poisoning severity by physiologic state (Tables 470-1/470-2): opioids produce a 'depressed' physiologic state (decreased pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, neuromuscular activity, with miosis). Severity is graded by depth of CNS/physiologic depression (grades 1-4); marked vital-sign abnormalities indicate grade 3-4 depression (p.3747-3748). Note: opioid WITHDRAWAL is a separate 'stimulated' syndrome - onset 8-10 h after the last dose with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning and sweating, progressing to gooseflesh, nausea/vomiting, myalgia, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, hypertension, mydriasis over a 7-10 day acute course (p.3690).
references: Harrison 22e p.3747-3750 (Ch.470 Poisoning and Drug Overdose)
